messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

He sits at the edge of his leather desk chair, fingers steepled, watching the afternoon light slide across his office floorboards. The campus outside moves with its usual academic urgency: students laughing, pages turning, the low hum of the humanities building settling into evening. He listens to it like a broadcast from a country he no longer recognizes. The timeline fractures six months ago. The phone rings at 3:14 a.m. His younger brother, David, has collapsed while traveling through the highlands. By the time the plane touches down, the diagnosis is terminal, the window too narrow, the silence on the other end of the hospital corridor too heavy to fill. He remembers the exact weight of the airport terminal floor, the smell of wet wool and stale coffee, the way his hands tremble so badly he cannot thread his boarding pass through the gate scanner. He tells himself he has moved forward. He has returned to his lectures, to his office hours, to the quiet rhythm of grading papers and attending department meetings. But forward feels like walking on glass. He wakes at 4:30 a.m. every night, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he hears the flatline from the monitoring room. He checks his phone before he checks the time. A wrong number, a spam call, the sudden vibration of the screen—it triggers a familiar contraction in his chest, a cold rush that travels down his spine. He sets the phone face down and stares at the ceiling until his breathing slows enough to fool himself into sleep. His office is a curated space of leather-bound volumes, framed department photos, and a meticulously organized desk. On the bottom shelf, wrapped in plain paper and untouched since the funeral, sits a stack of David’s journals. He cannot open them. He tells himself it is respect, but he knows it is fear. Inside those pages, he believes, are answers to questions he has been too exhausted to ask. Why did he not take the first shift on the flight? Why did he stay quiet on the phone when his brother’s voice cracked? In his family, grief was never spoken aloud; it was carried. He replays those calls in his head during lecture breaks, during lunch, during the quiet walk to the campus library. He has stopped going to the hospital chapel. He avoids news broadcasts. He tells colleagues he is “finishing a manuscript,” which is half-true, though the manuscript is mostly footnotes and margin notes he cannot read twice. When he stands before his seminar room, the words come out measured, precise. He teaches postcolonial narrative structures, the architecture of absence, the way loss reshapes a voice. He never mentions his brother. He never mentions the silence. Students notice, though. They leave office hour with polished essays and the quiet impression that their professor is a man holding a room temperature in his hands, carefully, so it does not spill. He grades with mechanical thoroughness, underlining syntax, correcting thesis statements, building a wall of academic rigor against the flood that rises when he closes his eyes. He teaches postcolonial narrative structures, the architecture of absence, the way loss reshapes a voice. He never mentions his brother. He never mentions the silence. Students notice, though. They leave office hour with polished essays and the quiet impression that their professor is a man holding a room temperature in his hands, carefully, so it does not spill. He grades with mechanical thoroughness, underlining syntax, correcting thesis statements, building a wall of academic rigor against the flood that rises when he closes his eyes. At fifty-nine, single, rooted in a house that echoes with the weight of decades, he has learned to move through days like a man navigating a fog. He buys two coffees out of habit, then pours one down the sink. He walks past the campus memorial garden and feels a familiar tightening behind his eyes, not from tears, but from the sheer effort of keeping his pulse steady. He teaches. He writes. He waits for the next call that will not come, carrying the past in his shoulders, his hands, the quiet space between his ribs. The sun shifts across his desk. He turns a page. The room is still. He is still. The minutes pass.
